title: Reliability-Aware and Anatomy-Preserving Replay for Continual Echocardiographic Segmentation
summary: Continual echocardiographic segmentation remains challenging due to catastrophic forgetting, domain shifts, and heterogeneous anatomical supervision. Existing continual-learning methods often struggle to preserve previously acquired knowledge while adapting to new imaging distributions, particularly under limited replay memory and incomplete anatomical annotations. To address these challenges, we propose the Reliability-Aware Replay Network (RAR-Net), a continual segmentation framework integrating multi-factor exemplar prioritization, protected task-aware memory, forgetting-conditioned adaptive replay, and structure-aware supervision. RAR-Net combines class, boundary, image, anatomical, and temporal reliability criteria to prioritize informative historical examples, while adaptive replay regulates their contribution during sequential training. Structure-aware supervision further reinforces previously learned anatomical knowledge when subsequent datasets provide incomplete annotations. Extensive experiments performed on CAMUS, CardiacNet, and EchoNet-Dynamic demonstrate that our RAR-Net achieves the highest final average accuracy among the evaluated continual-learning methods, with competitive historical knowledge retention and segmentation performance approaching the offline joint-training reference. These findings indicate that coordinating reliability-guided memory management, forgetting-conditioned replay, and anatomy-specific supervision can support knowledge retention and adaptation under the evaluated sequence of heterogeneous echocardiographic datasets.

title: GeoCANO: A Geometry-Conditioned Adaptive Neural Operator for Physical-Field Prediction on Varying Domains
summary: Industrial design requires repeated evaluation of candidate configurations. Integral performance measures alone do not resolve critical local phenomena, while high-fidelity simulation remains costly. Existing physical-field surrogates often couple geometry representation and coordinate evaluation through prescribed mesh topologies, limiting reuse across resolutions. We propose the Geometry-Conditioned Adaptive Neural Operator (GeoCANO), which maps a sampled complete three-dimensional geometry to a coordinate-dependent field function. An attention-based encoder extracts a geometry state from unordered surface coordinates. A multiresolution axis-factorized hash encoding and query-wise sparse mixture-of-experts decoder enhance multiscale expressiveness. GeoCANO constructs the field representation before introducing output coordinates, allowing one geometry encoding to be reused across regions without rebuilding the graph for each output topology. We evaluated GeoCANO on transonic aerodynamic-field prediction over complete aircraft configurations using a Reynolds-averaged Navier-Stokes dataset of 10,484 wing-body-nacelle geometries. For unseen configurations within the sampled design family, GeoCANO outperformed baselines in complete-surface prediction, high-gradient pressure reconstruction, and pressure-drag recovery. It reduced pressure-coefficient mean absolute error by 77.9% relative to the strongest baseline and retained an advantage over a finite range of wall-normal distances. Ablation studies showed that geometry-modulated coordinate encoding achieved comparable accuracy with substantially fewer parameters than conventional three-dimensional hash encoding. Routing analysis indicated spatially structured, query-dependent expert specialization. These results demonstrate a reusable continuous-coordinate representation for rapid physical-field evaluation over varying geometries.

title: Exact Volume-Preserving Diffeomorphic Shear Splitting: Continuous-Discrete Geometric Bounds, Reversible Memory Backpropagation, and Expressivity Frontiers in Volumetric Mapping
comment: 17 pages, 4 figures, 4 tables. Reversible PyTorch autograd engine with exact volume-preserving diffeomorphism guarantees
summary:
Incompressible diffeomorphic registration requires continuous spatial mappings that preserve local tissue volume (det(DΦ) = 1) without topological folding (det(DΦ) > 0). Standard velocity-field methods (SVF, LDDMM) approximate incompressibility via numerical ODE integration or soft penalties, exhibiting numerical volume drift (~10^-4 to 10^-1), iterative grid inversions, and linear backpropagation memory O(L * N_vox).
  We formulate an exact structure-preserving framework for 3D registration based on cascaded coordinate shears. By decomposing the divergence-free Lie algebra sdiff(Ω) into six coordinate-shear generators whose convective non-linearities vanish identically, each elementary stage integrates analytically to a closed-form triangular shear with det(DS_k) = 1 and exact machine-precision inverse requiring zero iterations and zero spatial interpolations. Multi-stage compositions generate the connected volume-preserving group SDiff_0(Ω). We establish: (i) an unconditional global diffeomorphism proof closing the Hadamard-Caccioppoli injectivity gap; (ii) a Dirichlet boundary confinement lemma; (iii) an anisotropic Riemannian similarity invariance; (iv) a Sobolev H^2 spectral budget preventing chaotic mixing; and (v) an exact reversible backpropagation engine eliminating O(L) trajectory storage (0.00 MB intermediate activations).
  We prove second-order O(h^2) sub-voxel convergence across 16^3 to 64^3 lattices and second-order trajectory accuracy for palindromic Strang splitting (468.1x error reduction vs. Lie-Trotter; drift |det(DΦ)-1| <= 2.22e-16). Execution is 2.1x-4.0x faster than SVF with 78.4% GPU memory reduction. On cardiac cine-MRI (ACDC, N=100) and brain MRI (OASIS-1, N=414), our model achieves competitive Dice (0.884 and 0.841) while strictly maintaining 0.0000% folding and zero volume drift.

title: Machine learning for trigger, reconstruction and generation
summary: Machine learning (ML) is increasingly embedded in every stage of the LHC data-processing chain, from event generation to final reconstruction. This contribution reviews the latest ML developments from the ALICE, ATLAS, CMS and LHCb collaborations that were made public in the year preceding LHCP2026, following the workflow of the experiments: event generation and detector simulation, real-time trigger selection, and online/offline reconstruction. Highlights include generative models that accelerate the simulation of specific ALICE detector components by up to six orders of magnitude, the CMS AXOL1TL and ATLAS GELATO unsupervised anomaly- detection triggers now operating in Run 3, a quantised Deep Sets jet tagger for the CMS Phase-2 Level-1 trigger, ML-based jet energy correction and flavour tagging at LHCb, the first empirical scaling laws for transformer-based flavour taggers in ATLAS, and several transformer and graph- based reconstruction algorithms (ATLAS GN3 flavour tagging and MaskFormer tracking, LHCb GarNet, CMS MLPF) developed for HL-LHC operation.

title: InterGS+: Inter-Frame Gaussian Splatting Compression with Geometry-Aware Transformer Prediction and Adaptive Residual Coding
comment: Accepted for poster presentation at the 2027 Data Compression Conference (DCC 2027)
summary: Dynamic 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) provides real-time photorealistic rendering, but representing each frame as irregular Gaussian primitives with high-dimensional attributes creates substantial storage and transmission cost. Exploiting temporal redundancy is challenging because Gaussian primitives do not preserve fixed identities across frames. We propose InterGS+, a lightweight post-hoc inter-frame codec that jointly improves temporal prediction and residual representation. Current-frame geometry is coded with G-PCC and reconstructed before prediction, enabling consistent temporal neighborhoods at encoder and decoder. Attributes are predicted using lightweight KNN and bilateral predictors together with a geometry-aware transformer for spherical-harmonic (SH) appearance, with per-Gaussian mode selection. Residual coding is adapted to each attribute: SH innovations are coded in a shared PCA domain using vector quantization with refinement, opacity and scale in activated gamma-companded domains, and rotation as canonicalized quaternion innovations using vector quantization and refinement. On MPEG dynamic sequences, InterGS+ achieves average BD-rate reductions of 45.48% over G-PCC Amd. 1 and 7.78% over InterGS-Lite, with corresponding BD-PSNR gains of 9.98 dB and 1.10 dB. Average decoding complexity is 0.049 ms/Gaussian, demonstrating efficient streamable dynamic 3DGS compression.

title: CEDVR: A virtual reality event display for CMS
summary: Collision event displays are widely used in high-energy physics (HEP) experiments, enabling researchers to visualize and debug raw and reconstructed event data, and to communicate aspects of individual events to broader audiences. Such event displays are typically viewed on a conventional two-dimensional computer screen. To enhance immersion and interactivity with CMS data, we have developed a virtual reality (VR) software package named CEDVR (for CMS Event Display in Virtual Reality) that uses widely-available VR headsets and hand controllers. This application provides an immersive detector-coordinate view and a novel, complementary LEGO-style view. CEDVR provides easy access to physics object properties and object filtering, and incorporates novel VR features for navigation and object selection. Compatible with consumer-grade Quest headsets, CEDVR is a useful visualization tool for CMS physicists, and contains built-in sample events that support educational and public outreach initiatives.

title: Ultra-Wideband Stacked Patch Antenna for D-Band Applications
summary: This article proposes a wideband stacked dual-patch antenna designed for D-band applications. The antenna is demonstrated with both wireless and dielectric waveguide (DWG) channels. The patch dimensions and spacings are chosen to ensure that the $10~dB$ return loss (RL) bandwidth covers the entire D-band ($110$--$170~GHz$). The antenna is fabricated on a seven-layer organic packaging technology. The patches are fabricated on layers 1 and 3 within a shielding cavity formed by closely spaced vias of $< λ/20$ pitch. The fabrication technology supports direct chip-level excitation of the antenna using a flip-chip packaging interface, and the design methodology for this feeding approach is outlined in the paper. In the fabricated design, however, a transition to the WR6 metallic waveguide with ($<~1~dB$) insertion loss (IL) is incorporated for feeding. This facilitates alignment and measurement of the structure using external test equipment. The full antenna and transition are integrated in a back-to-back configuration, achieving a measured $10~dB$ return loss bandwidth of more than $60~GHz$ ($110$--$170~GHz$) for the wireless link, thereby covering the entire D-band. To the best of our knowledge, this is the widest antenna bandwidth reported in the same frequency range. The measured peak gain is $8.5~dBi$ (35$^\circ$ H-plane $3~dB$ beamwidth) with a gain variation of $3.5~dBi$ within the operating bandwidth. For the dielectric waveguide configuration, the measured $10~dB$ RL bandwidth also exceeds $60~GHz$, fully encompassing the D-band. The simulated insertion loss coupling into the dielectric waveguide is $3.5~dB$. A 1-meter dielectric waveguide channel fed with the proposed antenna is measured. The overall channel exhibits a total insertion loss of $14.7~dB$, of which a simulated $3.5~dB$ at $140~GHz$ is attributed to the loss of each side that feeds the DWG.

title: Longitudinal-dither wavefront sensing: Calibration-free measurement of mode mismatch
summary: Mode mismatch between a gravitational-wave detector and the beams injected into it lowers the power stored in the arms and the level of squeezing. Correcting it requires the complex amplitudes of the three second-order modes, measured on a calibrated scale with the cavity on resonance at its operating power. Here we present a method that obtains a signal proportional to the mismatch by moving the beam on the wavefront sensors already used for alignment control. A longitudinal dither of the cavity adds to the resonant mode a reference field, which reaches the sensors through the same signal chains and so calibrates both the scale of this signal and the Gouy phases of the sensors and actuators, with no external calibration. We demonstrate the method on an optical cavity held on resonance in its operating state at input powers of 2 W and 62 W. At 2 W it yields an optical model that agrees with independent measurements in the mode content, and with the layout model in the actuator Gouy phase within its uncertainty of about $1^\circ$. At 62 W the thermally induced change of the eigenmode is decomposed into waist-size and waist-position changes. The method requires only components that every controlled cavity already possesses and enables continuous in situ monitoring of the mode matching in the operating state.

title: Characterizing Datasets to Anticipate Unsupervised Domain Adaptation Performance for Radiographic Pneumonia Detection
comment: 12 pages, 8 figures. Submitted to IEEE Journal of Biomedical and Health Informatics
summary:
Deep learning models for pneumonia detection from chest radiographs exhibit degraded accuracy when applied across institutions, which motivates Unsupervised Domain Adaptation (UDA). We observe that UDA performance depends on the properties of both the source and target datasets, and that performance gains are asymmetric with respect to dataset pairs. We investigate which structural properties of chest X-ray datasets are the most important predictors of UDA performance, and whether they can be measured before adaptation is attempted.
  Five chest radiograph datasets were characterized by the class separability of their features, obtained from one forward pass of a frozen DenseNet-121 and summarized by the Silhouette Score, with the Fisher Ratio as a supporting measure. All twenty directed source-target pairs were adapted with a Domain-Adversarial Neural Network (DANN), while direct transfer without adaptation was also evaluated. Seven published transferability estimators were computed on the same representation for comparison.
  We found that adaptation performance depended on both endpoints in opposite directions. More separable target datasets attained higher AUC scores ($r=0.934$, $p=0.042$), whereas more separable sources produced lower AUC scores ($r=-0.922$, $p=0.017$). The signed difference in separability tracked the signed difference in AUC between the two directions of a pair ($r=-0.932$, $p=0.017$) and identified the better direction in 10 of 10 pairs ($p=0.001$). The proposed descriptor was comparable to the best published estimators on target evaluation.
  Source and target datasets play opposite structural roles in adaptation: higher class separability makes a dataset easier as a test set but not as a training source. This framework can guide dataset selection for adaptation in low-resource settings without running full experiments.

title: Noncontact Chemical and Morphological Profiling in Liquid via Fiber-Based Micro-FTIR
summary: Liquid-phase mid-infrared (MIR) imaging is challenging due to the strong MIR light absorption of most liquid media. Existing liquid-phase MIR microscopy approaches overcame the background absorption using predominantly either ultrathin liquid cells or attenuated total reflection (ATR) setups. However, these designs introduce additional challenges, such as sample confinement, limited probe volume, probe perturbation, and/or lack of quantification capabilities. In this work, a fiber-based Fourier-transform infrared (FTIR) microspectroscopy method was developed to overcome the technical barriers of liquid-phase MIR characterization. By integrating a tapered fiber microprobe, a transmission-based optical setup, and a scanning stage, we achieved noncontact chemical and morphological profiling in liquid. The micro-FTIR capabilities were benchmarked by measuring a micropatterned photoresist substrate in water, obtaining quantitative spatial chemical distribution and morphological profiles with ~35 μm lateral resolution and nanometer-scale vertical detection limit. This noncontact, quantitative, liquid-phase micro-FTIR technique is promising for non-perturbative characterization of heterogeneous structures in liquids.

title: Compact Slow-Wave Hybrid Magnonics on Ultrahigh-Permittivity Substrates
summary: Hybrid magnonics based on spoof surface plasmon polaritons (SSPPs) enables strong, broadband magnon-photon coupling, but the centimeter-scale device footprints required at low gigahertz frequencies hinder integration. Here, we demonstrate miniaturized slow-wave hybrid magnonic devices using an ultrahigh-permittivity ceramic substrate ($\varepsilon = 140$). Owing to the inverse-square-root dependence of the SSPP plasma frequency on effective permittivity, the required corrugation finger length is reduced by nearly a factor of four compared with conventional microwave substrates. The ceramic is thick and brittle, and conventional thin-film processes cannot easily pattern thick, low-loss conductors on it. We overcome this challenge with additively manufactured electronics (AME). In a customized AME workflow, a multi-material inkjet printer first prints a dielectric fixture that holds and registers the ceramic. After the ceramic is loaded, the printer prints thick silver SSPP patterns directly onto it. Measurements on six printed devices with different finger lengths confirm the predicted geometry-frequency scaling. Moreover, the enhanced field confinement of the compact SSPP waveguide nearly doubles the magnon-photon coupling strength and yields ultrastrong coupling with $g/f_\mathrm{p} \approx 22\%$. Notably, this performance is achieved using a YIG film whose magnetic volume is more than an order of magnitude smaller than that employed in previous SSPP demonstrations. These results establish AME on ultrahigh-permittivity substrates as a practical route toward compact, strongly coupled hybrid magnonic devices.

title: Supersymmetry of Helmholtz waves
summary: Symmetry organizes physical laws, links conservation principles to transformations, and reveals connections between seemingly different systems. We show that Helmholtz waves support Witten supersymmetry through their spatial symmetries, without additional internal degrees of freedom. Reflection across the transverse horizontal axis induces a $\mathbb{Z}_{2}$ grading of the Euclidean algebra, whose odd generators supply charges connecting opposite-parity Cartesian and Bessel modes at equal separation eigenvalues. The Bessel model has an unpaired even zero mode, Witten index one, and unbroken supersymmetry for any rotation-axis position along the reflection line. We express all four separators through mixed supercommutators of displaced orbital-angular-momentum generators, establish Weber pairing through a spectral sign operator, and identify the obstruction to equal-eigenvalue Mathieu pairing at nonzero ellipticity. We extend our construction to multiple transverse shells and generate supersymmetric partner fields with a common Talbot recurrence. Gaussian apodization centered on the rotation axis gives finite-power fields and preserves our charge relations during exact forward propagation while modifying the ideal revival. Our framework may guide optical transformations between parity partners and the characterization of structured fields.

title: Studies of dual ions arriving time reconstruction in N$ν$DEx time projection chamber
summary:
The N$ν$DEx experiment aims to search for neutrinoless double-beta decay of \(^{82}\)Se with a high-pressure \(^{82}\)SeF\(_6\) negative-ion time projection chamber. In the assumed two-carrier model, the arrival-time separation of SeF\(_5^-\) and SeF\(_6^-\) can estimate the longitudinal coordinate without an external trigger. We compare FFT deconvolution and direct waveform fitting on simulated Topmetal-S charge-sensitive-amplifier waveforms.
  With the fixed amplifier response, direct fitting and FFT accepted 873 and 855 of 873 geometry-selected single depositions, respectively. On the 855 common events, the arrival-time separation RMSEs were 0.180 and 0.222 ms. Numerical depth calibration gave mean \(z\) residuals of 0.036 and 0.075 cm and RMSEs of 0.192 and 0.208 cm on 848 common events. With sampled CSA shaping, FFT accepted the same 855 waveforms and direct fitting accepted 866 of 873. On the four-way common sample of 855 events, the direct-fit separation RMSE was 0.180~ms with fixed shaping and 0.217~ms with sampled shaping. An accepted near-readout direct fit outside the FFT sample had a 184~ms separation error, giving an RMSE of 6.25~ms over all accepted sampled-response direct fits.
  With the fixed response, the full-track fit retained 1,185 of 1,810 observed pads in 100 selected Geant4 events. The median event-level depth RMSE was 0.184 cm. Subtracting each event's mean Monte Carlo residual gave a median event-centred RMS of 0.102 cm as a diagnostic of relative track shape. The absolute depth remains sensitive to the common event time. Validation with detector data is needed to assess the effects of diffusion, electronics noise, and inter-pad response.

title: N-Polar AlGaN/GaN Heterojunction Bipolar Transistor
summary: Heterojunction bipolar transistors based on the III-Nitride systems have significantly lower performance than field effect transistors due to challenges associated with p-type doping of the base. N-polar AlGaN/GaN HBTs can overcome these challenges by polarization-induced holes in the base and base-emitter interface. We experimentally demonstrate the first N-polar AlGaN/GaN heterojunction bipolar transistors (HBTs) grown by plasma-assisted molecular beam epitaxy on GaN substrate without emitter regrowth. The HBTs exhibit a peak current gain of approximately 15, peak differential current gain of approximately 18, and emitter-area-normalized peak current densities exceeding 20 kA/cm^2 and 66 kA/cm^2 for emitter areas of 10 x 10 um^2 and 3 x 10 um^2, respectively. The specific contact resistance for base is estimated 1.32 x 10^{-2} Ohm.cm^2. The open-base breakdown voltage is characterized ~63 V for a 300 nm collector without dielectric passivation. This work lays the foundation for future development of N-polar III-Nitride HBTs for next-generation RF applications.

title: Single-shot on-chip measurement of the modal Stokes parameters
summary: Integrated photonics has recently facilitated manipulating multimode partially coherent light in a compact mesh of Mach-Zehnder interferometers. A critical task in this context is on-chip reconstruction of the coherence matrix through a sequence of measurement configurations, thus giving rise to a speed bottleneck stemming from temporal delays in tuning on-chip phase shifts. Here we demonstrate single-shot reconstruction of the coherence matrix for two-mode partially coherent light by parallelizing the on-chip measurements of the modal Stokes parameters, thereby exchanging space for time. Although a larger chip area is required, the reconstruction is limited only by detection speed, thus potentially paving the way to real-time reconstruction of coherence matrices for applications in high-speed communications, cryptography, computation, and sensing.

title: Design, Testing and Calibration of the GAPS Experiment Si(Li) Tracker Readout ASIC: From the First Flight Campaign Toward the Second Mission Upgrade
comment: PhD thesis, University of Bergamo, PhD program in Engineering and Applied Sciences, defended January 2026. Advisor: Prof. Massimo Manghisoni. 203 pages, 126 figures, 27 tables
summary: The General Antiparticle Spectrometer (GAPS) is a balloon-borne experiment designed to perform three long-duration flights from Antarctica to search for low-energy cosmic antinuclei, in particular antideuterons, as an indirect signature of dark matter. Its detection method relies on the formation and decay of exotic atoms, identified through the emission of characteristic x-rays and the subsequent annihilation into secondary particles. At the core of the instrument is the silicon tracker, composed of lithium-drifted silicon detectors operated at -40°C and read out by a custom application-specific integrated circuit, SLIDER32, implemented in 180 nm CMOS technology. This thesis reports on the integration, calibration, and validation of the SLIDER32-based tracker readout electronics. Laboratory characterization of a tracker module with an Am-241 source and cosmic muons was complemented by calibration and testing of the full tracker in flight configuration, leading to the first x-ray spectrum acquisition from a Cd-109 source. These activities were part of the integration and testing phase for the first flight, culminating in the complete instrument assembly and validation during the 2024 Antarctic campaign. Building on this experience, the work presents the design and characterization of ANTARES4, a prototype integrated circuit in 65 nm CMOS technology conceived as an upgrade to SLIDER32. The chip integrates eight analog channels up to the shaping stage and implements dynamic signal compression based on dynamic-threshold MOS transistors, together with an improved detector leakage current compensation circuit at the preamplifier input. Its characterization provides a first validation of these design choices, laying the foundations for the next-generation tracker readout to be adopted in the second flight of the experiment.

title: Emission regimes and characteristic energy scales in reverse-biased 4H-SiC Schottky barriers: unified field-emission formulas and energy-dependent tunneling effective mass
comment: 40 pages, 12 figures, supplementary material included. Submitted to Jpn. J. Appl. Phys. A Japanese version is available at Jxiv, doi:10.51094/jxiv.7256
summary: Reverse leakage in 4H-SiC Schottky barrier diodes is analyzed using a current integral with Fermi-Dirac supply and WKB transmission. The ratio of the interface field to a critical field $F_c$ sets the depth of the thermionic-field-emission (TFE) saddle point. The Airy energy distinguishes the thermionic-tunneling crossover, the validity of the TFE formula, and the TFE/field-emission (FE) boundary, which generalizes to $c_1 k_B T \approx 1$ for arbitrary barrier shapes. Closed-form FE and TFE expressions are given for triangular and quadratic barriers; for the latter, the Padovani-Stratton formulas give 1.4-7.9 times (FE, $10^{19}$ cm$^{-3}$) and 2.5-3.6 times (TFE, low-doped layers, 300-433 K) the WKB current, whereas the present expressions agree within 15% and 2%. Applied to Ti/4H-SiC data (30-160 °C, 50-950 V), an energy-dependent tunneling mass from the complex band structure reduces the residual from 0.17 to 0.11-0.12 dex; it can be implemented in device simulation via the Franz two-band dispersion.

title: Phase matching of high-order harmonics driven by a combined coherent and bright squeezed vacuum field
summary: High-order harmonic generation (HHG) driven by non-classical light provides new insights into light-matter interactions and paves the way to quantum attosecond spectroscopy. Achieving phase matching is vital for generating bright HHG sources, while it has received comparatively limited attention in quantum-light-driven HHG. In this work, we investigate the phase matching of HHG driven by an intense coherent field combined with a weak bright squeezed vacuum (BSV) field, using a semiclassical ensemble of coherent-field realizations sampled from the Husimi-$Q$ probability distribution. We reveal the physical mechanism behind the distinct pressure dependence of the harmonic yields for odd, even and half-integer sidebands spectral components, as observed in our previous experiment [arXiv:2607.20941]. The simulations and phase-matching model demonstrate that the BSV-induced perturbation of the electron action phase could introduce an additional sub-cycle phase mismatch, such that the amplitude of sub-cycle bursts could be significantly modified by gas pressure after macroscopic propagation, even when the harmonic yield is near the optimum. The resulting amplitude asymmetry of sub-cycle bursts leads to a significant intensity contrast between half-integer sidebands harmonics, manifesting as distinct pressure dependence of their yields. Our findings reveal the phase-matching mechanism in two-color quantum-light-driven HHG, and suggest opportunities for macroscopic control of the non-classical HHG source.

title: Determining the electron-hole pair creation energy in a 4H-SiC p-n diode via X-ray spectroscopy
comment: Accepted for publication in JINST, 9 pages, 4 figures
summary: This paper reports on a measurement to determine the electron-hole pair creation energy in a 4H-SiC p-n diode. By measuring the spectra of several X-ray sources and comparing the response between the silicon-carbide diode and a commercial silicon diode, the electron-hole pair creation energy in 4H-SiC is determined to be (7.87 $\pm$ 0.09) eV. This is the first result obtained using X-ray spectra from several sources and including an estimate of the uncertainty. The result is in good agreement with studies of comparable devices.

title: Witnessing Gaussian Coexistence and Correlation-Ellipse Tomography
summary: Gaussian light is specified by second-order field moments, yet their hidden correlation geometry can demand higher-order intensity measurements. We establish a measurement hierarchy for "Gaussian coexistence", i.e., the simultaneous presence of cross covariance and cross pseudocovariance. For two zero-mean Gaussian modes with circular marginals, all unperturbed intensity moments of second or third order are blind to coexistence. In contrast, a balanced fourth-order residual provides a necessary and sufficient witness. Their identities, however, remain fundamentally ambiguous: recovering the two correlation strengths does not reveal which belongs to the covariance and which to the pseudocovariance. Unexpectedly, adding thermal fluctuations resolves this ambiguity: an independent, correlated thermal probe selectively modifies the covariance while leaving the pseudocovariance unchanged, allowing the two correlation strengths to be individually identified. Moreover, a coherent reference in only one arm then makes their relative phase accessible through third-order intensity correlation. Together, these measurements reconstruct a correlation ellipse and its Poincaré-sphere coordinates, determining the relative channel strengths and the ellipse orientation. The framework separates what intensity detection can witness, what thermal probing can identify, and what a single phase reference can orient, turning inaccessible Gaussian correlation structure into a quantitatively reconstructible geometry.

title: Theory of modulation instability for coupled microresonators
summary: Thanks to hybridization phenomena, coupled microresonator systems enable modulation instability (MI) of the continuous wave background field across all possible dispersion combinations: anomalous-anomalous, normal-normal, and anomalous-normal microrings. Here, using the Lugiato-Lefever model in the supermode basis for two coupled microresonators with arbitrary second-order dispersion coefficients, arbitrary losses, and coupling strength, we derive a general eigenvalue problem for the $4\times 4$ matrix. We consider the regime of resonance splitting, in which the pump couples only to one of the two supermodes, allowing us to obtain analytical expressions for the stationary continuous-wave field distributed over the coupled system. When the microresonators have similar geometry, the antidiagonal elements of the eigenvalue-problem matrix nearly vanish, and we obtain a fully analytical solution for the MI gain rate for the entire range of coupled microresonator devices. Finally, we investigate cases in which the analytical treatment must be supplemented with more accurate numerical solutions of the MI eigenvalue problem, though even then the analytical theory captures the main features of the four-wave mixing process and the gain-rate behavior.

summary: Mode mismatch between a gravitational-wave detector and the beams injected into it lowers the power stored in the arms and the level of squeezing. title: Mechanisms of turnkey soliton generation in self-injection-locked photonic-crystal ring resonators
summary: Turnkey generation of dissipative Kerr solitons in photonic-crystal ring resonators relies on the interplay between engineered mode splitting, self-injection locking, and modulation instability, yet the mechanism governing soliton initiation and number selection remains incompletely understood. We investigate this interplay using coupled Lugiato-Lefever equations with a self-consistent nonlinear self-injection-locking condition. Analysis of continuous-wave steady states and their locking stability reveals operating points accessible through feedback-induced transitions between split resonances. Evaluating modulation-instability gain at these points identifies conditions for comb initiation and links the dominant unstable sideband modes to soliton-number selectivity. Direct time-domain simulations corroborate the analysis, showing that appropriately chosen mode splitting enables highly repeatable single-soliton generation without external laser-frequency scans. The final soliton number is nevertheless shaped by subsequent nonlinear evolution and feedback-induced detuning changes, rather than by the initial instability alone. We also show that larger dispersion suppresses higher-order unstable modes and favors lower soliton numbers.

title: Temporal Soliton Waves in Modern Fiber Laser Systems
comment: This is the review article, which belongs to one of chapter for book: Handbook of Optical Fibers
summary:
This chapter provides a comprehensive survey of temporal soliton-wave
  in modern fiber systems. Temporal soliton waves constitute a broad class of nonlinear localized structures in modern fiber laser systems, arising from different balances among dispersion, nonlinearity, gain, loss,
  spectral filtering, and various forms of cavity coupling. We review the underlying theory, basic experimental findings, and practical methods for the generation, real-time characterization, and active control of soliton families, with a particular focus on recent progress reported for mode-locked fiber-laser platforms. The families covered in the chapter include dissipative solitons, soliton molecules (bound states), and dispersion-managed solitons. For each species, we focus on the pulse energy, duration, stationary and breathing states, and emerging intelligent (machine-learning-assisted) control strategies.

title: Competing Symmetry Breakings and Spontaneous Parity Restoration in Desynchronously Pumped Kerr Resonators
summary: Symmetry breaking is a cornerstone of nonlinear science, where stronger driving typically compounds parity loss across coupled degrees of freedom. Here, we uncover a counterintuitive symmetry-restoring transition driven by the competition between internal spontaneous polarization symmetry breaking (PSB) and external explicit temporal symmetry breaking (TSB) in desynchronously pumped Kerr resonators. Tuning pump-cavity desynchronization steers dissipative cavity solitons from pure PSB, through a robust hybrid symmetry-breaking (HSB) regime where both asymmetries coexist, into a pure TSB state accompanied by the abrupt, spontaneous restoration of polarization parity. Using collective-coordinate perturbation theory, we map the effective Ginzburg-Landau potential landscape and show that kinematic drift weakens local driving until a saddle-node bifurcation eliminates the temporal confining barrier. Corroborated by full Ikeda-map simulations across the phase boundary, our results demonstrate how driven-dissipative systems sacrifice internal order to satisfy external kinematic constraints, offering a general paradigm for competing order parameters in multidimensional nonlinear systems.

title: Tweezing microparticles by tightly focused optical skyrmionic fields
summary: The concept of skyrmions, once translated to the optical domain, provides a topological framework to investigate structured light-matter interactions. However, their practical use for the manipulation of material systems remains barely explored. Here, we experimentally demonstrate trapping and tunable orbital motion of dielectric microparticles in tightly focused skyrmionic polarization textures prepared using a compact spin-orbit optical element. We explore the tweezing capabilities at fixed topology either by varying the relative weights of the orthogonally polarized components or by switching between skyrmion and bimeron polarization textures. Vectorial focusing and optical-force calculations qualitatively reproduce the experimental observations. These results motivate extending skyrmionic light to the manipulation of micro-objects, including birefringent and chiral samples.

title: Toward light-controlled transverse Wigner ordering in attosecond electron beams
comment: 25 pages (13 pages main text including 3 figures, plus 12 pages Supplemental Material)
summary: Kinetic fluctuations and space-charge expansion hinder Wigner ordering in free-electron beams. Here we propose a laser-driven route toward transient, substrate-free Wigner ordering that combines photon-induced near-field electron microscopy (PINEM) attosecond bunching, synchronized magnetic focusing, and spatial preconditioning. Classical relaxation and zero-temperature fixed-node diffusion Monte Carlo trap benchmarks show that sixfold order survives quantum fluctuations from 1 T to sub-Tesla fields, defining ultrafast preparation targets.

title: Magnetometry and slow light in PT-symmetric cavity optomechanics
summary: The generation of optical higher-order sidebands, which produces new frequencies with regular spectral separation, holds significant promise for applications in optical communication and quantum metrology. We investigate second-order sideband generation and tunable slow-fast light effects in a parity-time (PT)-symmetric cavity optomechanics and propose an enhanced magnetometer scheme. We demonstrate that the PT-symmetric structure, an external magnetic field, and the photon tunneling strength provide powerful and flexible control over both the second-order sideband efficiency, as well as the broadening and switching of slow-fast light propagation. Operating in the PT-symmetry-protected phases, our magnetometer based on the second-order sideband achieves a theoretical sensitivity at the picotesla level, surpassing the performance of previous optomechanical approaches. Our results offer new strategies for magnetic field sensing and optical transmission control, paving the way toward applications in quantum sensing and optical information storage.

title: Quantum Tautochrone for photons and atoms
summary: The tautochrone problem, in which the travel time to a common point is independent of the starting position, has served as a foundational model in classical mechanics. Here we establish its quantum counterpart in engineered photonic waveguide arrays and atomic optical lattices, where nonuniform couplings drive photons and particles launched from different positions to converge simultaneously at a common site. Using higher-order correlation functions, we show that this quantum tautochrone effect holds for both bosons and fermions, with quantum statistics governing the character of the convergence: bosons converge onto the same site, while fermions, constrained by Pauli exclusion, gather at neighboring sites. For bosonic atoms, we further show how the tautochrone dynamics is shaped by lattice inhomogeneity, phase-space structure, and on-site interactions.

title: Dynamic tuning of anisotropy-induced quasi-bound-states-in-the-continuum in liquid-crystal integrated dielectric metasurfaces
summary: Symmetry-protected quasi-bound states in the continuum (qBICs) in all-dielectric metasurfaces can be excited either by introducing a geometrical asymmetry into the unit cell or by illuminating the metasurface under oblique incidence. To date, tuning the coupling strength of such qBICs to the continuum has mainly relied on control of the geometrical asymmetry. Here, we show that qBICs can also be induced in a symmetric dielectric metasurface by embedding the latter into an anisotropic birefringent medium, and that they can be actively tuned by either rotating the anisotropy axis of the medium or by varying the degree of anisotropy. We experimentally implement a corresponding system by embedding a highly symmetric silicon nanocylinder metasurface into a nematic liquid crystal (LC) cell. Importantly, the LC does not only provide the desired birefringence, but also dynamic control of its strength as well as of the orientation of its anisotropy axis in response to different external stimuli. Specifically, applying voltage across the LC cell, where the LC molecules are pre-aligned along one of the lattice directions of the metasurface, enables out-of-plane rotation of the anisotropy axis of the LC medium. Meanwhile, its birefringence can be tuned by changing the temperature. In our experiments, the coupling of the qBICs to the radiation continuum is first maximized by the application of 25 V across the LC cell at room temperature. We then systematically tune the temperature and show that the resonance depth of the qBIC modes, which is associated with their coupling strength to the continuum, of the qBIC modes increases monotonously with birefringence. Our findings establish anisotropy-induced qBICs in LC integrated dielectric metasurfaces as a promising platform for actively reconfigurable metasurfaces and their applications in displays, optical modulation and tunable photonic devices.

title: Propagation-tunable fractional Stokes skyrmions in conical refraction
summary: Conical refraction in a biaxial crystal generates Stokes textures whose finite-domain skyrmion number takes fractional values tunable through free-space propagation, while the underlying azimuthal winding remains unchanged. For a circularly polarised Gaussian input, the skyrmion number is governed by the boundary Stokes parameter, $N_\mathrm{sk}=[1-s_3(R_\mathrm{cut},Z)]/2$. Six-state polarimetry reveals fractional values of 0.523, 0.565 and 0.266 in the Lloyd, Poggendorff and Raman regions, respectively, in close agreement with Belsky-Khapalyuk-Berry predictions of 0.530, 0.550 and 0.250, and reproduces the predicted longitudinal evolution. Conical refraction thus provides a passive route to propagation-tunable fractional Stokes skyrmions, in which continuously evolving polarisation geometry coexists with a fixed topological winding.

title: Witnessing Gaussian Coexistence and Correlation-Ellipse Tomography
summary: Gaussian light is specified by second-order field moments, yet their hidden correlation geometry can demand higher-order intensity measurements. We establish a measurement hierarchy for "Gaussian coexistence", i.e., the simultaneous presence of cross covariance and cross pseudocovariance. For two zero-mean Gaussian modes with circular marginals, all unperturbed intensity moments of second or third order are blind to coexistence. In contrast, a balanced fourth-order residual provides a necessary and sufficient witness. Their identities, however, remain fundamentally ambiguous: recovering the two correlation strengths does not reveal which belongs to the covariance and which to the pseudocovariance. Unexpectedly, adding thermal fluctuations resolves this ambiguity: an independent, correlated thermal probe selectively modifies the covariance while leaving the pseudocovariance unchanged, allowing the two correlation strengths to be individually identified. Moreover, a coherent reference in only one arm then makes their relative phase accessible through third-order intensity correlation. Together, these measurements reconstruct a correlation ellipse and its Poincaré-sphere coordinates, determining the relative channel strengths and the ellipse orientation. The framework separates what intensity detection can witness, what thermal probing can identify, and what a single phase reference can orient, turning inaccessible Gaussian correlation structure into a quantitatively reconstructible geometry.

title: Topological terahertz fields from tunable vectorial currents
summary: Future information processing calls for photonic architectures with greater capacity, intrinsic resilience to noise, and direct integration with quantum materials and devices. Topological light pulses have recently emerged as promising candidates to meet these demands, yet the complexity underlying their unique properties also makes them challenging to generate, tune, and fully resolve in space and time. Here, we generate and actively tune topological light fields through transient vectorial currents in an optoelectronic metasurface. Incident linear polarization steers the local direction of photocurrents in graphene via nanoplasmonic resonators with triangular symmetry, while a global winding pattern enables continuous tuning between compressional and circulating charge flows. Under ultrafast excitation, these currents radiate single-cycle terahertz toroidal pulses spanning electric- and magnetic-dominant modes with dynamically evolving skyrmion textures. Full spatiotemporal mapping and reconstruction provide a complete visualization of the toroidal structure of light, directly tracing the closed field surfaces while continuously tracking skyrmion number and helicity throughout a single cycle. These results connect two-dimensional vectorial currents to rich three-dimensional electromagnetic field structures, while establishing a versatile integrated platform for higher-dimensional photonic information processing and emerging material spectroscopies.

title: A library-based approach for inverse reconstruction of cavity depth using angle-resolved cathodoluminescence
summary: In nanofabrication processes, accurate metrology is a crucial step for obtaining control over the required critical dimensions in a device. Traditionally, scanning electron microscopy (SEM) is used to obtain high resolution measurements of the lateral dimension, but obtaining depth information on a thick sample is more complex. In this work, we use angle-resolved cathodoluminescence (AR-CL) spectroscopy to resolve this third dimension. Using 30 keV electrons in the SEM, CL is created at the bottom of a micrometer scale cavity milled in a gold surface. We show that reflections of the CL off the cavity sidewalls produce an interferogram which is a sensitive probe for the cavity geometry. The interferograms can be modelled using the finite-difference time-domain method, and we demonstrate that a neural network trained on a library of these simulated patterns can be used to reconstruct the cavity depth. This approach establishes a proof of concept for AR-CL based depth reconstruction within a prescribed geometry and could form a route towards advanced three-dimensional metrology of complex nanostructures.

title: Nonreciprocal state-selective splitting of eigenstates at a polarization exceptional point
summary: Non-Hermitian photonic systems can be engineered to exhibit exceptional points (EPs), where eigenvalues and eigenstates coalesce. Although perturbations near EPs have mainly been characterized through eigenvalue splitting, the branch-resolved evolution of the coalesced eigenstates under a tunable reciprocity-breaking perturbation remains less systematically explored. Here, we show that tunable nonreciprocal coupling can produce state-selective splitting of the coalesced eigenstates near a second-order polarization EP. Using temporal coupled-mode theory, we find that the corresponding off-diagonal perturbation produces a triangular Hamiltonian in the circular-polarization basis. In the ideal limit, one eigenstate remains pinned to the EP state, whereas the other is continuously reoriented by the perturbation. In a realistic scattering system, residual reverse-polarization conversion weakly displaces the nominally pinned branch, resulting in quasi-pinning. We numerically demonstrate this mechanism in a reflective magneto-optical metasurface supporting a circular-polarization EP of the reflection matrix near 582 nm. Full-wave simulations show that a perpendicular magneto-optical bias leaves one reflection eigenstate close to the EP state while reversibly displacing the other on the Poincare sphere. This asymmetric eigenstate evolution manifests as a magnetically tunable circular-dichroic reflection response. Our results establish a nonreciprocal route to state-selective eigenstate control near polarization EPs.

title: AI-Assisted Topological High-Harmonic Spectroscopy for Characterizing Crystal Symmetries and Nonlinear Responses
summary: Structured light has emerged as a unique tool for probing nonlinear light-matter interactions. Particularly interesting is its interaction with anisotropic media, such as crystalline materials, whose anisotropic responses encode information about their electronic properties. Recently, topological high-harmonic spectroscopy was introduced as an all-optical approach to extract the anisotropic nonlinear response of graphene from harmonic spatial intensity profiles. Here, topological high-harmonic spectroscopy is combined with artificial intelligence (AI) to retrieve the anisotropic non-linear response and crystal symmetry of atomically thin materials. A convolutional neural network is trained and validated to learn the inverse mapping between harmonic far-field intensity profiles and the nonlinear response of materials exhibiting different rotational symmetries. Comparisons with microscopic high-harmonic-generation simulations demonstrate the accurate retrieval of distinct effective nonlinear responses in single-symmetry crystals, such as single-layer graphene and bilayer graphene with different stacking orders, and in crystals exhibiting multiple symmetry components, such as monolayer hexagonal boron nitride. Macroscopic high-harmonic-generation simulations assess the robustness and applicability limits of the technique. These results establish AI-assisted topological high-harmonic spectroscopy as a fast, contactless tool for characterizing nonlinear optical responses and crystal symmetries without phase-resolved measurements, opening prospects for applications to complex systems such as polycrystals and van der Waals heterostructures.

title: Heat Reduction in Erbium-Doped Microresonator
summary: We investigate anti-Stokes fluorescence in a 106-micrometer-diameter silica whispering-gallery-mode microresonator coated with erbium-doped sol-gel, assessing its potential for reduced optical heating. Near-infrared fluorescence spectra acquired under pulsed excitation near 1.55 micrometers exhibit a mean emitted photon energy above the pump photon energy. Measurements over a temperature range of 25 to 62 degrees Celsius show that the mean fluorescence photon energy increases with externally controlled temperature. The measured pump-wavelength dependence is consistent with an absorption-weighted spectral model, which predicts an optimum near 1562.65 nm for the investigated spectral figure of merit. Resonance-dependent emission patterns further motivate a dual-frequency pumping scheme using two higher-order whispering-gallery modes. Calculated time-averaged field profiles indicate that complementary modal distributions can provide more uniform excitation near the equator. These results characterize spectral conditions relevant to fluorescence-based heat reduction and suggest a route toward improved spatial pump coverage. Demonstrating net optical refrigeration requires additional measurements of absorbed pump power and an independent thermal readout.

title: Packing the Bragg sphere: complete three-dimensional photonic band gaps at the refractive index of polymers (1.55)
summary: Complete 3D photonic band gaps have so far been found only at refractive-index contrasts of about 1.9 and above, reached by rod-connected diamond lattice structures. Reciprocal-space design of quasiperiodic structures recently achieved considerable emission attenuation at much lower contrasts [L. Maiwald et al., Adv. Optical Mater. 10, 2100785 (2022)]. Here we implement systematic search and reciprocal-space design of periodic 3D structures with complete band gaps, solving a discrete optimization problem on an integer lattice. A gap above a high band needs the strongest Fourier components of the dielectric close to the Bragg sphere of that band. Crystals with large cells, started from Fourier peaks at the vertices of a polyhedron on this sphere and optimized against densely refined band edges, open complete gaps down to an index contrast of 1.55, that of common polymers against air. A rational approximant of an icosidodecahedron gave the most efficient location of the Fourier peaks among the polyhedra tested. Numerical calculations confirm the gaps over a resolution series, with band edges searched over the whole Brillouin zone. The best designs are connected porous networks, suited to a microwave test with printed polymer. A rigorous bound, valid for any structure, does not exclude gaps at lower index, and the next rational approximants of the icosidodecahedron, whose Bragg zones match bands 576 and 2440 almost exactly, point to where gaps at even lower contrast may be sought.

title: Recipe for near-unity efficient frequency conversion via transient molecular modulation
summary: Frequency transduction technologies are an essential element for interfacing devices operating at distinct spectral regions. Specifically, the conversion of weak signals between different wavelengths is a fundamental requirement of quantum networks, where conversion efficiency is critical for preserving the statistical properties of light. In this regard, molecular modulation in gas-filled hollow-core fibers offers a promising approach for highly-tunable linear frequency conversion of classical and quantum light. However, recent experimental studies in this subject have struggled to overcome a saturation in conversion efficiency to about 70%, which, although high, might impair the faithful transfer of quantum properties upon conversion. In this work, we discuss a route to surpass this limitation that identifies the key factors to consider for obtaining quantum efficiencies exceeding 99%. These results might pave the way to viable fiber-based quantum transduction schemes for next-generation quantum networks.

title: Integrated lasing and dual-band gain in neodymium-implanted silicon nitride
summary: Lasers at wavelengths near 1 micrometer are used in quantum technologies, precision metrology, and sensing. Rare-earth gain at these wavelengths in photonic integrated circuits can reduce the size and enable the scalable fabrication of these lasers. We fabricate neodymium-based integrated waveguide amplifiers and a ring laser using neodymium-implanted LPCVD silicon nitride. The photonic integrated circuits were fabricated on a 200 mm commercial wafer platform, and individual dies were implanted with neodymium ions. We show that the amplifiers provide gain in two bands around wavelengths of 920 nm and 1100 nm, and we show lasing in a ring resonator. This demonstrates that neodymium-implanted LPCVD silicon nitride is a suitable gain material for integrated lasers.
